hints: Look closely at what is shared here: many ribosomes are all attached to the same single mRNA molecule at the same time.
Remember that one mRNA codes for one polypeptide, so ask yourself what happens to output if several ribosomes read that same message one after another instead of just one.
walkthrough:
**Spot the structure**

This chain of ribosomes on one mRNA is called a polysome or polyribosome. Think of it like several readers reading the same instruction sheet, just starting at slightly different points.

All of them are reading the exact same mRNA code.

**Apply the translation rule**

Each ribosome translates the mRNA codons into the same amino acid sequence to make the same polypeptide. Having many ribosomes does not change the message, it just copies it many times in parallel.

**Pick the advantage**

One ribosome alone would make one copy at a time. Many ribosomes together make many identical copies at the same time, so the cell gets lots of that needed protein much more rapidly.

options.A: Not correct. Because all ribosomes are on the same mRNA, they all make the same polypeptide, not different ones.
options.B: Not correct. Each ribosome still needs a full set of tRNAs to bring amino acids, so more ribosomes actually use more tRNAs, not fewer.
options.C: Not correct. The size of the polypeptide is set by the length of the mRNA coding sequence, not by how many ribosomes are attached.
options.D: Correct. Well done. Multiple ribosomes translate the same mRNA simultaneously, so many identical polypeptides are finished in the time one would take alone.
